The '''Kentucky coffeetree''' ('''''Gymnocladus dioicus'''''), also known as '''American coffee berry''', '''Kentucky mahogany''', '''nicker tree''', and '''stump tree''',<ref>{{Cite book|author=Beasley, V.|chapter=Toxicants that Affect the Autonomic Nervous System (and, in some Cases, Voluntary Nerves as Well)|date=9 August 1999|title= Veterinary Toxicology|publisher=International Veterinary Information Service|location=Ithaca, New York|chapter-url=http://www.ivis.org/advances/beasley/cpt2g/ivis.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060822151433/http://www.ivis.org/advances/Beasley/Cpt2G/IVIS.pdf|archive-date=22 August 2006|url-status=live}}</ref> is a [[tree]] in the subfamily [[Caesalpinioideae]] of the legume family [[Fabaceae]], native to the [[Midwestern United States|Midwest]], [[Upper South]], [[Appalachia]], and small pockets of [[New York (state)|New York]] in the [[United States]] and [[Ontario]] in [[Canada]]. The seed may be roasted and used as a [[Coffee substitute|substitute for coffee]] beans; however, unroasted pods and seeds are toxic.<!-- see text for more detail --> The wood from the tree is used by [[cabinetmaker]]s and [[carpenter]]s. It is also planted as a [[urban forestry|street tree]].

From 1976 to 1994, the Kentucky coffeetree was the state tree of [[Kentucky]], after which the [[tulip poplar]] was returned to that designation.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.netstate.com/states/symb/trees/ky_tulip_poplar.htm|title=Kentucky: Adoption of the Kentucky State Tree|publisher=NETSTATE|access-date=2013-06-12}}</ref>

==Description==
{{More citations needed section|date=February 2021}}
The tree varies from {{convert|18|to|21|m|ft|sp=us}} high with a spread of {{convert|12|–|15|m|ft|sp=us}} and a trunk up to {{convert|1|m|ft|abbr=off|sp=us|spell=in}} in diameter. The tree grows at a medium rate with height increases of anywhere from {{cvt|12 to 24|in|cm}} per year.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.arborday.org/trees/treeguide/TreeDetail.cfm?ItemID=819|title=Kentucky Coffeetree Tree on the Tree Guide at arborday.org|website=www.arborday.org|access-date=2017-08-11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url= https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=a872| title=Gymnocladus Dioicus| access-date=2026-06-20}}</ref> A 10-year-old sapling will stand about {{convert|4|m|ft|abbr=off|sp=us}} tall. It usually separates {{convert|3|to|4+1/2|m|ft|abbr=off|sp=us}} from the ground into three or four divisions which spread slightly and form a narrow pyramidal head; or when crowded by other trees, sending up one tall central branchless shaft to the height of {{convert|15|–|21|m|ft|abbr=on}}. Branches are stout, pithy, and blunt; roots are fibrous.<ref name=Keeler>Keeler, Harriet L. (1900). ''Our Native Trees and How to Identify Them''. New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, pp. 109–112.</ref>

The Kentucky coffeetree is a moderately fast-growing tree, and male trees are often grown in parks and along city streets for ornamental purposes. The tree is typically fairly short-lived, healthy trees living from 100 to 150 years.<ref name="UK-Ext">{{Cite web|title=Kentucky Trees: Gymnocladus dioicus (Kentucky Coffeetree), Pea Family (Fabaceae) |publisher=Cooperative Extension Service, College of Agriculture, University of Kentucky|url=http://www.uky.edu/Ag/Horticulture/kytreewebsite/pdffiles/GYMNOprint.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090124055027/http://www.uky.edu/Ag/Horticulture/kytreewebsite/pdffiles/GYMNOprint.pdf|archive-date=24 January 2009|url-status=live}}</ref> The Kentucky coffeetree sheds its leaves early during the fall and appears bare for up to 6 months. The naked appearance of the tree is reflected through the Kentucky coffeetree's Greek genus name, which means "naked branch".<ref name=Barnes>Barnes, Wagner et al. (1977). ''Michigan Trees''</ref> Like the [[Sumac]], branches are absent of fine spray; smaller branches are thick and lumpish. Because of the absence of smaller branches and its later leafing, the French in Canada named it '''Chicot''', "stubby". The expanding leaves are conspicuous because of the varied colors of the leaflets; the youngest are bright pink, while those which are older vary from green to bronze.<ref name=Keeler />
[[File:Kentucky Coffee-tree Gymnocladus dioicus 3264px.jpg|thumb|Bark of the Kentucky coffeetree]]
[[File:Kentucky coffee-tree flowers.png|thumb|Flowers]]

The bark is ash-gray and scaly, flaking similarly to [[black cherry]], but more so. The trees are [[plant sexuality|dioecious]], and the [[fruit]] is a hard-shelled bean in heavy, woody, thick-walled pods filled with sweet, thick, gooey pulp. Pod length ranges from {{convert|5|to|10|in|mm}}; unfertilized female trees may bear miniature seedless pods. The beans are commonly thought to contain the [[toxin]] [[cytisine]], although this has yet to be confirmed in a study.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Spaeth |first1=John P. |last2=Thieret |first2=John W. |title=Notes on "Coffee" from the Kentucky Coffeetree (Gymnocladusdioicus, Fabaceae) |date=2004 |journal=SIDA, Contributions to Botany |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=345–356 |jstor=41969015 |issn=0036-1488}}</ref>

* [[Bark (botany)|Bark]]: Tan or dark gray, deeply fissured, surface scaly, often with prominent narrow ridges. Branchlets at first coated with short reddish down.
* [[Wood]]: Light brown; heavy, strong, coarse-grained; durable in contact with the ground, takes a fine polish. [[Specific gravity]], 0.6934; weight of cubic foot, {{convert|43.21|lb|abbr=on}}.
* Winter [[bud]]s: Minute, depressed in downy cavities of the stem, two in the axil of each leaf, the smaller sterile. Bud scales two, ovate, coated with brown [[tomentum (botany)|tomentum]] and growing with the shoot, become orange green, hairy and about one inch long, before they fall.
* [[Leaf|Leaves]]: [[Alternate leaf|Alternate]], [[bipinnately compound]], ten to fourteen pinnate, lowest [[pinna (botany)|pinnae]] reduced to [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]], the other seven to thirteen [[Vernation|foliate]]. One to three feet long, eighteen to twenty-four inches broad, by the greater development of the upper pairs of pinnae. Leaf stalks and stalks of pinnae, are [[terete]], enlarged at base, smooth when mature, pale green, often purple on the upper side. Leaflets [[Glossary of leaf morphology#ovate|ovate]], two to two and one-half inches long, wedge-shaped or irregularly rounded at base, with wavy margin, acute apex. They come out of the bud bright pink, but soon become bronze green, smooth and shining above. When full grown are dark yellow green above, pale green beneath. In autumn turn a bright clear yellow. [[Stipule]]s leaf-like, lanceolate, serrate, deciduous.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gymnocladus dioicus (Kentucky Coffeetree, Kentucky Coffee Tree) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/gymnocladus-dioicus/ |access-date=2023-01-06 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref>
*Winter twigs are very stout and dark reddish brown to green brown in color; the pith is very thick and salmon pink to brown in color. The terminal bud is absent, and the lateral buds are small, bronze in color, and appear to be partially sunken beneath the bark of the twig. The leaf scars are very large, heart shaped with 3 to 5 conspicuous bundle scars. The flowers are dioecious (male and female flowers on separate plants). The female flowers are 8 to 12 inches long, greenish white in color, appear in early summer, and are quite fragrant. The male flowers are about half the size of the female flowers.<ref name="Kentucky Coffeetree">{{Cite web|url=https://naturalresources.extension.iastate.edu/forestry/iowa_trees/trees/kentucky_coffeetree.html|title=Kentucky Coffeetree|website=Natural Resource Stewardship|date=March 2019 |language=en|access-date=2020-04-15}}</ref>
* [[Flower]]s: June. [[Dioecious]] by abortion, terminal, greenish white. [[Staminate flower]]s in a short [[raceme]]-like [[corymb]] three to four inches (75–100 mm)  long, [[pistillate flower]]s in a raceme ten to twelve inches (250–300 mm)  long.
* [[Calyx (botany)|Calyx]]: Tubular, hairy, ten-ribbed, five-lobed; lobes valvate in bud, acute, nearly equal.
* [[Corolla (botany)|Corolla]]: [[Petal]]s five, oblong, hairy, spreading or reflexed, imbricate in bud.
* [[Stamen]]s: Ten, five long and five short, free, included; [[filament (botany)|filaments]] thread-like; [[anther]]s orange colored, {{linktext|introrse}}; in the pistillate flower small and sterile.
* [[Pistil]]: Ovary superior, sessile, hairy, contracted into a short style, with two stigmatic lobes; ovules in two rows.
* [[Fruit]]: [[Legume]], six to ten inches (150–250 mm)  long, one and one-half to two inches wide, somewhat curved, with thickened margins, dark reddish brown with slight glaucous bloom, crowned with remnant of the styles. Stalks an inch or two long. Seeds six to nine, surrounded by a thick layer of dark, sweet pulp.<ref name=Keeler />
* [[Fruit|Rooting Habit]], "Tap Root in proportion like a carrot". A seedling tree grows many times in root length to its growth upward in height. The Kentucky coffee tree is not commonly offered in the nursery trade because the taproot makes the tree somewhat difficult to transplant. Being in the Legume family the roots fix nitrogen in the soil.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a9IxAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA383|title=Report of the Iowa State Horticultural Society, for the Year ...|last=Society|first=Iowa State Horticultural|date=1910-01-01|publisher=The State|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.uaex.edu/yard-garden/resource-library/plant-week/kentucky-coffee-tree.aspx|title=University of Arkansas, Division of Agriculture Research and Extension, Plant of the Week, Kentucky Coffee Tree.|last=Klingaman|first=Gerald|date=February 14, 2003|website=Kentucky Coffee Tree|publisher=University of Arkansas|access-date=2016-10-07|archive-date=2016-10-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161007223037/http://www.uaex.edu/yard-garden/resource-library/plant-week/kentucky-coffee-tree.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref>
*[[Soil]]: Prefers rich, moist soils in floodplains, terraces, ravines, coves, and lower slopes.<ref name="Kentucky Coffeetree"/>

[[File:Gymnocladus-dioicus.jpg|thumb|upright|Fruit]]

==Taxonomy==
''Gymnocladus'' is derived from the [[Ancient Greek]] {{lang|grc|κλάδος}} (''kládos'') "branch" and {{lang|grc|γυμνός}} (''gumnós'') "naked" and refers to the stout branchlets unclothed with small twigs.

It is one of five species in the genus ''Gymnocladus'', and the only one native to [[North America]]; the other four being native to South, Southeast and Eastern [[Asia]].

The name is sometimes hyphenated as 'coffee-tree'; the form 'coffeetree' here is as used officially by the [[United States Forest Service]].

==Distribution==
The Kentucky coffeetree is widely distributed, but considered a rare tree species. "Rare species are those that are so uncommon that they should be monitored to determine whether their populations are becoming threatened."<ref name=Barnes />

The tree's native range is limited, occurring from [[Southern Ontario]], Canada and in the United States from [[Kentucky]] (where it was first encountered by Europeans) and [[Connecticut]] in the east, to [[Kansas]], eastern [[Nebraska]], and southeastern [[South Dakota]] in the west, to southern [[Wisconsin]] and [[Michigan]]<ref name=Barnes /> in the north, and to northern [[Louisiana]] in the south. It is planted as an urban shade tree across the United States and eastern Canada, including California.{{Citation needed|date=March 2021}} It has a [[disjunct population]] in [[Central New York]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://arboretum.harvard.edu/stories/exploring-the-native-range-of-kentucky-coffeetree/|title = Exploring the Native Range of Kentucky Coffeetree|date = 16 August 2018}}</ref>

The trees occur either in the form of widely dispersed individuals, or as small colonial groups with interconnected root systems. This tree is typically found in floodplains and river valleys, but is also sometimes seen on rocky hillsides and limestone woods. In the northeastern part of its range, seemingly natural groves of this tree are actually associated with known prehistoric village sites. In some parts of its range, this tree may be used as an indicator of the presence of limestone or of calcareous soils.{{Citation needed|date=March 2021}}

The Kentucky coffeetree is considered an example of an [[evolutionary anachronism]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Ecological impacts of the late Quaternary megaherbivore extinctions|journal = New Phytologist|date = 2014-03-01|issn = 1469-8137|pages = 1163–1169|volume = 201|issue = 4|doi = 10.1111/nph.12576|first = Jacquelyn L.|last = Gill|pmid=24649488| bibcode=2014NewPh.201.1163G }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title = The Ghosts of Evolution: Nonsensical Fruit, Missing Partners, and Other Ecological Anachronisms.|last = Barlow|first = Connie|publisher = New York: Basic Books.|year = 2000|isbn = 978-0-465-00551-2|url-access = registration|url = https://archive.org/details/ghostsofevolutio00conn}}</ref> The tough, leathery seed pods are too difficult for many extant animals to chew through (in addition to being poisonous) and they are too heavy for either wind or water dispersal. It has been hypothesized that the tree would have been browsed upon by now-extinct mammalian megafauna,<ref>Zaya, D.N., Howe, H.F. The anomalous Kentucky coffeetree: megafaunal fruit sinking to extinction?. Oecologia 161, 221–226 (2009). https://doi.org/10.1007/s00442-009-1372-3</ref> which ate the pods and nicked the seeds with their large teeth, aiding in germination. This behavior is seen among [[African elephant]]s eating ''Fabaceae'' relatives in Africa. Because of this, its prehistoric range may have been much larger than it has been in historical times. Today, in the wild, it only grows well in wetlands, and it is thought that only in such wet conditions can the seed pods rot away to allow germination in the absence of large herbivores.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://www.americanforests.org/magazine/article/trees-that-miss-the-mammoths/|title=The Trees That Miss The Mammoths|first= Whit |last=Bronaugh|year=2010|journal= American Forests|volume=115|issue=Winter|pages=38–43}}</ref> It is protected in some but not all parts of the Canadian province of Ontario.<ref name="Ontario-Reg">{{cite web|title=Ontario Regulation 60/26 made under the Species Conservation Act, 2025|url=https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/r26060 |date=March 26, 2026|publisher=Government of Ontario|access-date=2026-05-15}}</ref>

==Uses==
{{More citations needed section|date=February 2021}}
[[File:Kentucky coffee tree full.JPG|thumb|upright|Kentucky coffeetree (upright trunk) at Minnesota Landscape Arboretum]]

===Cultivation===
''Gymnocladus dioicus'' is considered well-suited to urban environments, as it is tolerant of poor soils, has extreme drought tolerance, and is not vulnerable to serious insect infestations or disease problems.<ref>Carstens, J.D.; Schmitz, A.P. 2017. Kentucky coffeetree, Gymnocladus dioicus (L.) K. Koch: Current abundance in nature and prospective persistence. In: Sniezko, Richard A.; Man, Gary; Hipkins, Valerie; Woeste, Keith; Gwaze, David; Kliejunas, John T.; McTeague, Brianna A., tech. cords. 2017. Gene conservation of tree species—banking on the future. Proceedings of a workshop. Gen. Tech. Rep. PNW-GTR-963. Portland, OR: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Pacific Northwest Research Station. p. 92.</ref> It is cultivated by specialty tree [[plant nursery|plant nurseries]] as an [[ornamental tree]] for planting in [[garden]]s and [[park]]s. The peculiarly late-emerging and early-dropping leaves, coupled with the fact that the large leaves mean few twigs in the winter profile, make it a tree that is ideal for urban shading where winter sunlight is to be maximized (such as in proximity to [[renewable energy|solar]] hot-air systems).

It is often planted because of its unique appearance and interesting character.<ref name=Keeler /> There are several Kentucky coffeetrees at [[Mount Vernon]], in the gardens along the path leading up to the house of [[George Washington]].

Trees prefer a rich moist soil, such as bottom lands.<ref name=Keeler />  Their growth is largely unaffected by heat, cold, drought, insects, disease, road salt, ice, and alkaline soil.
Kentucky coffeetree is easy to grow from seed. Filing the seedcoat by hand with a small file, and then soaking the seeds in water for 24 hours will ensure rapid germination. [[plant propagation|Propagation]] is also easy from dormant [[root cutting]]s from December through March.

The Kentucky coffeetree is typically found on "alluvial soils of river and flood plains and nearby terraces".<ref name=Barnes /> Here it may be locally abundant and form large [[clonal colony|clonal colonies]], reproducing by shoots sprouting from roots.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stubbendieck |first1=James L. |last2=Milby |first2=Jessica L |title=Legumes of the Great Plains an illustrated guide |date=2021 |publisher=U of Nebraska Press |location=Lincoln |page=17 |isbn=978-1-4962-2458-3}}</ref>

===Food===
The beans of the tree were eaten, after roasting, in the [[Meskwaki]] (Fox), [[Ho-Chunk]] (Winnebago) and [[Pawnee people|Pawnee]] Native American cultures.<ref name="auto">{{cite web|last1=Moerman|first1=Dan|title=Native American Ethnobotany Database|url=http://herb.umd.umich.edu|website=Native American Ethnobotany Database|publisher=University of Michigan|access-date=9 August 2014}}</ref>

The Meskwaki also drank the roasted ground seeds in a hot beverage similar to coffee.<ref name="auto" /> The common name "coffeetree" derives from this latter use of the roasted seeds, which was imitated by settlers because it seemed a [[Coffee substitute|substitute for coffee]],<ref name="USDA">{{Cite web |url=https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/cs_gydi.pdf |title=Kentucky Coffeetree (''Gymnocladus Dioicus'') |last1=Row |first1=John M. |last2=Geyer |first2=Wayne |date=2007 |website=Natural Resources Conservation Service |series=Fact Sheets & Plant Guides |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture |language=en |access-date=23 October 2012 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241121143615/https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/cs_gydi.pdf |archive-date=21 November 2024}}</ref> especially in times of poverty, similar to [[chicory]]. The European colonialists, however, considered it inferior to real coffee:

{{cquote|When Kentucky was first settled by the adventurous pioneers from the Atlantic states who commenced their career in the primeval wilderness, almost without the necessaries of life, except as they produced them from the fertile soil, they fancied that they had discovered a substitute for coffee in the seeds of this tree; and accordingly the name of coffee-tree was bestowed upon it. But when communication was established with the sea-ports, they gladly relinquished their Kentucky beverage for the more grateful flavor of the Indian berry; and no use is at present made of it in that manner.<ref name=Keeler />|||[[Andrew Jackson Downing]]}}

The roasted seeds can be eaten like sweet chestnuts.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Gymnocladus+dioica | title=Gymnocladus dioica Kentucky Coffee Tree PFAF Plant Database }}</ref> Usefully, the fruits can be collected and picked up from the tree or ground at any time during fall, winter, and spring.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Orn5YBjJvS8C&dq=%22Kentucky+coffeetree%22%2B%22fruit%2B%22winter%22&pg=PA578 | title=The Woody Plant Seed Manual | page= 578 | date=2008 | publisher=U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service | isbn=978-0-16-081131-9 }}</ref>

====Toxicity====
Caution should be used when consuming, as unroasted or only partially roasted beans and pods are considered poisonous and are reputed to contain the alkaloid [[cytisine]].<ref name=USDA/> The pods, preserved like those of the [[tamarind]], can be eaten and are slightly aperient (laxative).<ref name="nie">{{Cite NIE|wstitle=Gymnocladus|year=1905}}</ref> Many sources claim that roasting the seeds for a certain length of time can reduce or eliminate the cytisine thought to be in them, but this is not based on scientific evidence. There are however, many anecdotal accounts of people drinking a coffee-like drink made from the seeds without suffering any adverse health effects, although most reported the taste to be unpleasant.<ref name=":0" />

The plant is toxic to some animals<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.library.uiuc.edu/vex/toxic/kentucky/kentucky.htm|title=Kentucky Coffee Tree – Plants toxic to animals – Veterinary Medicine library at U of Illinois|work=uiuc.edu|access-date=2008-05-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080706072443/http://www.library.uiuc.edu/vex/toxic/kentucky/kentucky.htm|archive-date=2008-07-06}}</ref> and may intoxicate dogs.<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1892/0891-6640(2005)19[599:kctiia]2.0.co;2 | title = Kentucky Coffee Tree Intoxication in a Dog with Cerebellovestibular Signs, Bradycardia, Hypotension, and Hypoglycemia | date = 2005 | last1 = Troxel | first1 = Mark T. | last2 = Poppenga | first2 = Robert H. | journal = Journal of Veterinary Internal Medicine | volume = 19 | issue = 4 | pages = 599–601 | pmid = 16095181 }}</ref>

===Culture===
In addition to use as a food, the seeds of Kentucky coffeetree were used by [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]] for ceremonial and recreational purposes. Seeds were used as dice in [[games of chance]] that were common in eastern tribes. It is likely that indigenous community members carved patterns on coffeetree seeds used in ceremonial dice games, which also served to scarify the seeds and prepare them for germination.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kentucky Coffeetree |url=https://silverrunforestfarm.org/nursery/kentucky-coffee-tree |access-date=2023-02-03 |website=Silver Run Forest Farm |language=en-US}}</ref> The seeds were also used in jewelry. The importance of the Kentucky coffeetree to Native Americans undoubtedly contributed to its dispersal.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.uwsp.edu/forestry/StuJournals/Documents/NA/avannatta.pdf|last=VanNatta|first=Andrew R.|year=2009|title=Ecological Importance of Native Americans Culture to the Kentucky Coffee Tree (''Gymnocladus dioicus'')|publisher=University of Wisconsin Stevens Point|access-date=2013-07-17}}</ref>

''Gymnocladus dioicus'' is used as a street tree as far north as [[Québec City]], [[Québec]]. It resists harsh winters and de-icing salts.

===Woodworking===
The wood is used both by [[cabinetmaker]]s and [[carpenter]]s. It has very little [[Sapwood (wood)#Heartwood and sapwood|sapwood]].<ref name="nie" />

==Notable specimens==
{{More citations needed section|date=February 2021}}
A specimen with a height of {{convert|26|m|0}} was referenced in La Turpinerie, commune of [[Geay, Charente-Maritime|Geay]], a short distance from the [[Charente (river)|Charente]] in south-west France, growing in a typical calcareous soil (see Minutes of Congrès international de sylviculture de Paris, June 1900). Cut during the 20th century, it had a circumference of {{convert|2.8|m|0}} and was the tallest in the country at this time.

A Kentucky coffeetree, said to have been brought to the [[UK]] in 1812, stands in [[Mountsfield Park]] in the [[London Borough of Lewisham]].<ref name="londongardensonline1">{{cite web |url=https://londongardenstrust.org/conservation/inventory/site-record/?ID=LEW039 |title=London Gardens Online |publisher=London Gardens Online |date=1905-08-07 |access-date=2013-07-15 |archive-date=2016-03-04 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304084102/http://www.londongardensonline.org.uk/gardens-online-record.asp?ID=LEW039 }}</ref>

A Kentucky coffeetree found in the Will Rogers Park in [[Amarillo, Texas]] has been confirmed by Texas A&M Forest Service to be the largest of its kind in [[Texas]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://abc7amarillo.com/news/local/kentucky-coffeetree-in-amarillo-confirmed-to-be-largest-of-its-kind-in-texas | title=Kentucky coffeetree in Amarillo confirmed to be largest of its kind in Texas| date=2016-01-11}}</ref> It has a circumference of 92 inches, a height of 51 feet, and a crown spread of 52 feet.

A Kentucky coffeetree lives in Rhode Island in the [[Roger Williams Park Zoo]] at 1000 Elmwood Avenue, Providence.

At the [[U.S. Space & Rocket Center]] in [[Huntsville, Alabama]], 19 Kentucky coffeetrees are planted in the Apollo courtyard prior to entry into the museum.

In 2022, the Tree Board for the town of Hillsborough, North Carolina, selected a grove of Kentucky coffeetrees as its 2022 Treasure Tree. Originally the grove was mis-identified as a part of a program to remove invasive species, but the North Carolina Forest Service helped to confirm the proper identification of the trees.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tree Board Spotlights Kentucky Coffeetree Grove |url=http://www.hillsboroughnc.gov/news/news/2022/5/18/1266/tree-board-spotlights-kentucky-coffeetree-grove-with-treasure-tree-designation.html |access-date=2022-06-05 |website=www.hillsboroughnc.gov |language=en |archive-date=2022-05-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220518173331/https://www.hillsboroughnc.gov/news/news/2022/5/18/1266/tree-board-spotlights-kentucky-coffeetree-grove-with-treasure-tree-designation.html }}</ref>

The largest Kentucky coffeetree in [[New Hampshire]], at 91 ft tall, is on the campus of [[Dartmouth College]].<ref>https://unhcoopext.maps.arcgis.com/apps/Shortlist/index.html?appid=bc24f6238db1475e9d6bc3ef2d061c0f New Hampshire Big Tree Map</ref>

Kentucky coffeetrees can be found in [[Central Park]] in New York City.<ref>{{cite web | title=Kentucky Coffeetree | url=https://www.centralparknyc.org/plants/kentucky-coffeetree }}</ref>
